name: Brick
lede: Brick is the dark orange-red of fired clay, a color so tied to its material that cities, dye shops and dress manuals all used the word long before anyone fixed a swatch to it.

sections.title: The color of fired clay
sections.body:
Brick is the deep orange-red of a baked clay brick, a color Paterson also files under the old adjective *lateritious* [1]. His entry for *brick-red* adds a regional note: in the United States the term means a brownish or yellowish red [1]. Related words from the same family are *testaceous*, for the reddish-brown of unglazed tiles and flowerpots, and *adobe*, a pinkish red probably named for the sun-dried bricks of Latin America [1].

The color is less fixed than the word suggests. Albers observes that real bricks run through beige, yellow and orange, and on through ochre and brown to a deep violet, so one wall can hold many "brick" colors [2]. The swatch here is a dark, orange-leaning red, near [[chinese-red]], [[sweet-brown]] and [[burnt-umber]] [12].

Of the 7,500 color names that Deane Judd's survey at the National Bureau of Standards had identified, Garfield reports, 149 came from common things, and brick red is the example he gives [3].

sections.title: A city of red
sections.body:
Pastoureau argues that ancient Rome was not the white marble city of films and postcards [4]. Houses and ordinary buildings were mostly baked brick in every shade of red, and brick and tile together made Rome a red city, as were the other major cities of the empire [4]. He calls the white image a false one [4].

China had a similar pairing of walls and roofs: palaces of red brick under glazed yellow tile were reserved for the emperor and his family, and Europeans came to link China with yellow [5].

Not every "red" place is red because of brick. Pastoureau notes that Red Square in Moscow was called red in the time of the czars, before the Communist regime, and not for its brick buildings but because it was thought the city's most beautiful square [6]. A myth is easy to start from a coincidence of colors.

sections.title: Brick as a dye and a dress code
sections.body:
Brick-red was what a dyer got when madder went slightly wrong. Greenfield writes that madder reds usually leaned orange, so dyers often landed on corals, russets and brick reds, and only dyers in the Ottoman Empire, India and other Eastern countries could reliably get a rich red [7]. That is the dye behind [[flower:madder|madder]] at its most ordinary.

In the 1850s the same quiet reds had a social use [8]. English fashion manuals condemned scarlet and crimson as vulgar, yet judged dark reds, brick reds and maroon safe for a lady, above all a married one [8]. Brick red was the permitted red.

Other names for the shade come from places and materials. St Clair's glossary gives *Pompeian red* as a dark brick red, from the houses uncovered at Pompeii, and *Morocco* as a brick red that began as the color of painted leather [9]. Our [[pompeian-red]] is a cousin at ΔE 9.7 [12].

sections.title: Brick-red in the paint box
sections.body:
As a mixed color, brick red goes back to the first systems of color names. In 1769 Schäffer's chart of reds gave compartment 76, brick red, as a mixture of minium, lead white, orpiment and English red [10]. In his Wernerian list Jameson changed the red section's *brick red* to *tile red*, and Syme's chart later carried *tile red* as number 82 [10][11]. The brick became a tile, and the name moved.

Chemists used the word as a description too. Mercuric oxide made by precipitation could be brick red or orange-yellow, according to Salter in 1869 [13]. A mercury chromate pigment came in a dark brick-red variety and a violet-tinged one, according to Riffault in 1874 [13]. Catechu extract could be turned brick-colored with lead salts [13].

Bricks were also a swindler's filler. St Clair reports that French madder was accused of being adulterated with everything from brick dust to oats [14]. Balfour-Paul lists brick dust among the substances used to add weight to indigo [15].

sections.title: Seeing brick
sections.body:
Albers gives an exercise from his own class, after Bezold: the same light red bricks laid up with white mortar look much lighter than when laid up with black [2]. The brick's color depends on its neighbors, so a red wall seen at a distance is as much about the mortar as the clay.

Neighbors can also clash. The dealer Vollard recalled the painter Sérusier telling him, in a Paris street, that when he saw him in a brick-colored overcoat beside a woman in a violet coat, the two colors "screamed", and he felt ill [16]. If you want to see why, stand a brick wall next to anything violet.

At the oddest end of perception, Galton recorded a subject who saw the numeral 3 as a pale brick red [17].

sections.title: Brick and Brick Red
sections.body:
Two entries in our data have nearly the same name and are not the same color. The swatch on this page is Brick, #A03623, a dark red-orange that comes from the xkcd color survey of 2010 and our own app, with no earlier record and an origin undocumented in our data [12]. [[brick-red]] is a different swatch, #CB4154, a brighter and pinker red that Wikipedia traces to Crayola; the two are ΔE 14.7 apart [12]. Ridgway's plate color for brick red, #915248, is greyer and browner again [12].

The Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 gives 1667 as the first recorded use of *brick red* [12]. Treat that as a cataloguer's date and not a measurement of when anyone first said it.

In Japanese the nearest traditional name is *edocha*, "Edo brown", a red-brown [12].

sections.title: Brick in paintings
sections.body:
Brick is one of the more common named colors in old paintings, and it peaks in the Quattrocento [18]. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 569 contain it on at least 5 per cent of the canvas [18]. From the 1400s, 91 of 945 paintings contain it, which is 4 times the rate expected from the same museums [18]. The decade with the highest share is the 1390s, with 5 of 25 [18]. We cannot say from the data why, and photographs of aged paintings are not a pigment test.

The largest single share belongs to a Sienese work of 1440, *Payment of Salaries to the Night Watchmen in the Camera del Comune of Siena*, where it covers about half the surface [18]. The painting with the best-known name among the top six is Titian's [[painting:nga-41638|Cardinal Pietro Bembo]] from 1539, about a third brick-colored [18]. Among the painters who use it at the highest rates in the archive are [[painter:pontormo|Pontormo]], [[painter:albrecht-durer|Dürer]] and [[painter:sandro-botticelli|Botticelli]] [18].

In Nepal and Tibet it also stands out, in 3 of 25 and 4 of 47 works [18].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 569 contain this brick (within ΔE 6 of the swatch, on at least 5 per cent of the canvas, as photographed), a rate of 2.4 per cent [18].

By century: 91 of 945 paintings from the 1400s, 113 of 2,231 from the 1500s and 113 of 6,394 from the 1600s [18]. Pontormo has it in 3 of 13 works, Dürer in 6 of 47, Caravaggio in 5 of 47 and Botticelli in 4 of 48 [18]. 

The word *brick* in printed English peaks in the 1910s, but it also means the object, so it is not a clean color count and we do not lean on it [19]. These are photographs of paintings, not pigment tests, and screen colors are approximate.
